description: Prisma Client: which types are clients of the database, and what each client operation reads and writes.

rules.description: PrismaClient, as @prisma/client exports it, is a client of the database; so is a project class that extends it, as a NestJS PrismaService does.
rules.why: A call on a client's model delegate, prisma.user.findMany(...), is SQL the client sends to the table of that model.

examples.source:
import { PrismaClient } from '@prisma/client';
export class PrismaService extends PrismaClient {}

import { PrismaClient as Db } from '@prisma/client';
export class Store extends Db {}
examples.why: the import is matched by what the package exports, not by the local name

examples.source:
import { PrismaClient } from './my-own-client';
export class NotPrisma extends PrismaClient {}
examples.why: a class of that name from another module is not Prisma's

rules.description: PrismaService, as the nestjs-prisma package exports it, is a client of the database: the package declares it as a class extending PrismaClient.
rules.why: nestjs-prisma-starter injects nestjs-prisma's PrismaService; the source never shows that it is a PrismaClient, because it is in a package.

library.declares: export class PrismaService extends PrismaClient<Prisma.PrismaClientOptions, 'query' | 'info' | 'warn' | 'error'> implements OnModuleInit
library.source: nestjs-prisma, lib/prisma.service.ts, re-exported by lib/index.ts, read on main (github.com/notiz-dev/nestjs-prisma); nestjs-prisma-starter pins 0.22.0-dev.0

examples.source:
import { PrismaService } from 'nestjs-prisma';
export class Db extends PrismaService {}

rules.description: What each Prisma Client model operation is, and what part each argument plays: select returns the fields set to true (a value that is neither true nor false MAY be returned, read at run time), where and cursor filter by the fields they name (through the combinators AND, OR and NOT), orderBy, distinct, by and the aggregates read theirs, data, create and update write theirs, and include reaches relations. A key naming a compound unique or id (schema.prisma's @@unique/@@id) is read through the model's own compounds, never by splitting the key. A relation is followed into its model: in include or select as a find of its own (true is its whole row), in a filter through some, every, none, is and isNot (or a to-one filter written straight), _count as the related rows it counts, and in data as the nested writes it names, each with what it does to the related rows and to the link. $extends on a client makes a client, and an extension with a query component, or one not read, may change what a call sends; an extension Prisma.defineExtension makes is read where the same method holds it.
rules.why: Prisma Client's model API (prisma.io/docs/orm/reference/prisma-client-reference): a find without select returns every scalar field of the model, include returns every scalar field of the related model, and a nested write (create, connect, connectOrCreate, set, disconnect, update, updateMany, upsert, delete, deleteMany) acts on the related rows and on the link between the two. Client extensions (prisma.io/docs/orm/prisma-client/client-extensions): $extends returns a new client, and its query component intercepts the operations it names.

examples.args: { where: { email: e }, select: { id: true, name: false } }
examples.why: a field selected false is not returned

examples.args: { where: { OR: [{ email: e }, { name: n }] } }
examples.why: no select: every scalar field is returned

examples.args: { where: { id }, data: { name: n, posts: { create: [] } } }
examples.why: a nested write reaches another table, and says so

examples.args: { where: { accountId_date: { accountId, date } }, create: { accountId, date, value }, update: { value } }
examples.why: a compound unique key reads through the model's own compounds, not by splitting the key on _

examples.args: { where: { id_email: { a: 1, b: 2 } }, select: { id: true } }
examples.why: a named compound (@@unique([a, b], name: "id_email")) means a and b, never the id and email a split on _ would guess
a filter held in a variable has fields only the running program knows
a spread argument: which fields, and whether all of them are returned, is not known
a computed top-level key: which argument this call sends is not known, so it is not read as a select and the whole row is not claimed either
a select value that is neither true nor false MAY be returned: the field is not dropped and not claimed EXACT, it goes to mayReads
include returns every column of the related model, and the relation is followed into it

examples.args: { where: { id }, select: { email: true, posts: { where: { published: true }, select: { title: true } } } }
examples.why: a relation in a select is a find of its own on the related model: its where and its select are read there

examples.args: { select: { id: true, _count: { select: { posts: { where: { published: true } } } } } }
examples.why: _count counts the related rows a relation reaches, filtered by its own where
a relation filter reads the related model's fields it filters on
a to-one relation filter may be written straight, with no is

examples.args: { where: { id }, data: { posts: { create: [{ title: t }], deleteMany: { published: false } } } }
examples.why: each nested write is followed: a create writes the related row and sets the link, a deleteMany deletes the rows its filter reads

examples.args: { data: { title: t, author: { connect: { id: userId } } } }
examples.why: connect finds the related row by a unique field and sets the link: the related row is read, not written
an include value only the running program knows MAY read the relation: followed, and marked may, never claimed for certain
